source_text: Duos Ponticus deos adfert, tamquam duas Symplegadas naufragii sui, quem negare non potuit, id est creatorem, id est nostrum, et quem probare non poterit, id est suum, passus, infelix, huius praesumptionis instinctum de simplici capitulo dominicae pronuntiationis, in homines non in deos disponentis exempla illa bonae et malae arboris, quod neque bona malos neque mala bonos proferat fructus, id est neque mens uel fides bona malas edat operas neque mala bonas. languens enim — quod et nunc multi, et maxime haeretici — circa mali quaestionem, unde malum, et obtusis sensibus ipsa enormitate curiositatis inueniens creatorem pronuntiantem: ego sum, qui condo mala, quanto ipsum praesumpserat mali auctorem et ex aliis argumentis, quae ita persuadent peruerso cuique, tanto in creatorem interpretatus malam arborem malos fructus condentem, scilicet mala, alium deum praesumpsit esse debere in partem bonae arboris bonos fructus. et ita in Christo quasi aliam inueniens dispositionem solius et purae benignitatis, ut diuersae a creatoris, facile nouam et hospitam argumentatus est diuinitatem in Christo suo reuelatam modicoque exinde fermento totam fidei massam haeretico acore desipuit. habuit et Cerdonem quendam informatorem scandali huius: duo facilius duos deos caeci perspexisse se existimauerunt. unum enim non integre uiderant. lippientibus etiam singularis lucerna numerosa est. alterum igitur deum, quem confiteri cogebatur, de malo infamando destruxit, alterum, quem commentari conitebatur, de bono praeferendo construxit. has naturas quibus disposuerit articulis, per ipsas responsiones nostras ostendemus.
pass_a_gloss: Ponticus brings forward two gods, as it were two Symplegadas of his own shipwreck, which he could not deny, that is the creator, that is ours, and which he will not be able to prove, that is his own, having suffered, unhappy, the impulse of this presumption from a simple chapter of the Lord's pronouncement, disposing of those examples in humans, not in gods, of the good tree and the bad tree, because neither a good tree produces bad fruits nor a bad tree good fruits, that is neither a good mind nor good faith produces bad works nor bad ones good works. For he was weak, which also now many are, and especially heretics, around the question of evil, whence evil, and with obtuse senses, by the very enormity of curiosity, finding the creator pronouncing: I am he who creates evils, as much as he had presumed the author of evil, and from other arguments, which thus persuade each perverse person, so much had he interpreted the bad tree producing bad fruits in the creator, clearly bad, he presumed there must be another god in the part of the good tree producing good fruits. And thus in Christ, as if finding another disposition of sole and pure kindness, so that it is diverse from the creator's, he easily argued a new and foreign divinity revealed in his Christ, and with a small leaven, he corrupted the whole mass of faith with heretical bitterness. He also had a certain Cerdon as an informer of this scandal: two gods were more easily perceived by the blind as two. For they had not seen one god entirely. Even to the blind, a single lamp is numerous. Therefore, he destroyed one god, which he was forced to confess, by defaming evil, and he constructed another god, which he was attempting to comment on, by preferring good. We will show through our own responses the natures which he disposed of in these articles.
pass_b_english: Ponticus drags out two gods like the twin Symplegades that wrecked his ship: the Creator, our God, whom he cannot deny, and his own deity, whom he will never prove. He suffered this catastrophe, poor wretch, because he let a single, simple passage from the Lord's teaching — the parable of the good and bad tree, applied to human beings, not gods — drive him to the presumption that a good tree cannot bear bad fruit nor a bad tree good fruit; in other words, a good mind or faith cannot produce evil works, nor an evil mind good works. He stumbled, as many do now, especially heretics, over the problem of evil — where does it come from? — and, senses dulled by the sheer bulk of his own curiosity, he latched onto the Creator's declaration: "I am the one who creates evil." The more he had already presumed the Creator to be the author of evil, and the more other arguments that seduce every perverse mind reinforced that view, the more he read the bad tree bearing bad fruit — clearly evil fruit — into the Creator, and concluded there simply had to be another god to serve as the good tree bearing good fruit. Spotting in Christ what looked like an entirely different disposition, one of sheer, unmixed kindness that contrasted with the Creator's, he easily argued a new, alien divinity revealed in his Christ, and with that pinch of leaven he soured the entire batch of faith with heretical bitterness. He also had a certain Cerdo as the instigator of this scandal: two blind men thought they could more easily perceive two gods than one, because they had never seen the one God whole; even to the bleary-eyed, a single lamp looks like many. So he demolished the God he was forced to confess by slandering evil, and built up the god he tried to invent by exalting the good. We will expose the natures he has assigned to these articles through our own responses.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex syntax of the Latin text. Pass A provides a literal gloss, while Pass B provides a fluent rendering that preserves all nuances of the original, including the metaphor of the Symplegades, the distinction between the Creator and the 'other' god, and the reference to Cerdon. The translation of 'languens enim' as 'He stumbled' (Pass B) or 'For he was weak' (Pass A) correctly captures the sense of being in a state of spiritual/intellectual distress. The scripture allusion regarding the trees is correctly identified as a parable/pronouncement. No omissions or contradictions found.
